gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the NAS makers measure power under different conditions: QNAP's TS-264 draws 18.288 W with its disks asleep, more than the 16.98 W Synology lists for the DS225+ with its disks working. At the August 2026 US residential rate of 18.16¢/kWh, running one of these NAS units 24/7 costs about $10 to $46 a year in electricity, depending on the model and on whether the disks ever sleep.
standout_why: ChatGPT ran no searches and got no results, so there were no rival pages to compare against. Its answer gives an unsourced range of '$20–60 incremental' a year for electricity. It names no wattage, no model and no rate, and it does not say that each maker measures power under different conditions. Our current page says 'about $1 a month power' for the DXP2800. That matches a disks-asleep or idle figure, not a NAS that is serving a public site around the clock. The range itself is partly in ChatGPT's answer already. What is new is the per-model figures, where they come from, and the footnote saying the makers' numbers can't be compared directly.
decides: This confirms that the case for a home NAS is not about saving money. Electricity alone for a 2-bay NAS running 24/7 is about $27 a year for the DS225+ and about $46 a year for the TS-264 at their 'access' or 'typical' figures. That is about as much as, or more than, a year of the cheapest shared hosting before renewal. The current page's '$1 a month' should become a range, with a note that disks serving a database-backed site may not get to sleep. Ranked by power, the DS225+ is the lowest-cost NAS choice and the TS-264 the highest. The TS-264's figures are about 70% higher, but QNAP tested with every bay filled and didn't name the drives.

findings.label: Power draw, access / HDD hibernation (maker)
findings.note: The spec page does not name the drives or how many were installed for the power figures. It only links to a Synology KB article on its method, and that article would not render for me. Annual cost at 18.16¢/kWh: access 16.98 W × 8,760 h = 148.7 kWh ≈ $27.01; hibernation 6.08 W × 8,760 h = 53.3 kWh ≈ $9.67.

findings.label: Memory, default / maximum
findings.value: 2 GB / 6 GB (2 GB + 4 GB) DDR4 non-ECC
findings.note: Synology states that non-Synology memory modules void the full product warranty and technical support. Running WordPress + MariaDB in 2 GB alongside DSM is tight. The supported upgrade is Synology's own 4 GB module.

findings.label: Warranty
findings.value: 3 years, extendable to 5 years (Extended Warranty Plus, North America/Europe, bought within 90 days)
findings.note: A hardware warranty, not an uptime guarantee.

findings.label: Power draw, operating typical / disk standby (maker)
findings.note: QNAP's footnote: 'Tested with drives fully populated'. It does not name the drive model. Its disk-standby figure (18.288 W) is higher than Synology's access figure (16.98 W), so the two makers' numbers are not measured the same way. Annual cost at 18.16¢/kWh: 29.086 W → 254.8 kWh ≈ $46.27; 18.288 W → 160.2 kWh ≈ $29.09.

findings.label: Memory default / max; warranty
findings.note: Celeron N5095, 4 cores, up to 2.9 GHz.

findings.label: Power draw, idle / maximum (measured by ocinside.de)
findings.note: Ocinside measured 'approx. 7 watts' at idle and 34.7 W maximum under a combined CPU, RAM and disk stress test. The review mentions 3.5-inch HDDs in RAID 1 but does not link them to the power readings. Annual cost at 18.16¢/kWh: 7 W → 61.3 kWh ≈ $11.14; 34.7 W → 304.0 kWh ≈ $55.20. The current page's '$1 a month' matches this idle figure.
